en: The Lamp Illuminating the Excellence of Vīraśaivism is now commenced.
Salutations to Śrī Gaṇeśa. Victorious is the illustrious King of Gurus.
The Vīraśaivotkarṣapradīpikā (The Lamp Illuminating the Excellence of Vīraśaivism) is now commenced.
I bow to Śrī Śiva, whose nature is existence, consciousness, and bliss, and who is the cause of all.
I bow to the one named Mahāliṅga, who is to be worshipped by those seeking liberation. || 1 ||

I bow to my Guru, who is the beginningless and stainless moving embodiment (Jaṅgama), devoted to the supreme bliss of excellent virtues, and who bears the celebrated name Toṇṭada Siddha Maheśvara in this world. || 2 ||
The embodiment of divine play, consisting of the beginningless moving world,
is the illustrious Toṇṭasiddheśvara, whose exaltedness was attained through the instruction received from the surging waves of his own unrestrained and generous glances of compassion.

May the ascetic Śrī Śāntavīra, the slayer of Mura, grant you stainless awakening as he properly proclaims the doctrines suitable for his own followers, which are appropriate for the illustrious Vīraśaiva tradition. || 3 ||
He has become, on all sides, a preeminent vessel for the abundant and true compassion of peaceful, heroic, and venerable masters.
I bow to that Guru, Siddha, and Preceptor who, possessing detachment, dwelt upon the surface of the earth. || 4 ||
He has attained the glory of Śiva through the grace of the masters of yoga, the perfected ones, and the spiritual preceptors.
Devoted to the awakening of the truth, the teacher Cannabasavārya shines in the city of nectar. || 5 ||
The wise and virtuous one named Muragha questioned such a guru according to his desire.
"Tell me that supreme truth, which is of such a nature and is esteemed by the virtuous. (6)
Thus speaking, he who is virtuous and named Muraghāta [the slayer of Mura] offered a hymn of praise to his Guru, consisting of a pair of questions and their respective answers, in due order.
"Expanding a work that follows the Vedas and Agamas, I shall speak; listen," he said with joy.

By means of the distinction between knowledge (*jñāna*) and action (*kriyā*) as propounded by the Siddhānta scriptures— which encompass the six stages (*ṣaṭsthala*) within their one hundred and one unsurpassed stages (*ekottaraśatasthalāni*), which serve as the supreme means for attaining liberation in the form of identity with the Great Liṅga (*mahāliṅgaikya*), and which are distinguished by the five modes of conduct (*pañcācāra*) and the eight enclosures (*aṣṭāvaraṇa*) renowned in all the Vedas, Āgamas, and Purāṇas.

And by means of a mind single-mindedly devoted to the worship and adoration of the *iṣṭaliṅga* (the chosen liṅga) and the *prāṇaliṅga* (the vital liṅga), which constitute the limbs and parts of the locus divided into six types— namely, the finger-liṅga, the body-liṅga, the devotion-liṅga, the power-liṅga, the hand-liṅga, and the mantra-liṅga— which serve as the modes for presenting the category of material form (*rūpapadārtha*), and which are based upon the contemplation of the meaning of the words of the oral instruction.
The illustrious Vīraśaiva, endowed with the knowledge of qualified non-duality (viśiṣṭādvaita), is the most excellent of all. || 8 ||
For it is said in the Śāṅkarasaṃhitā: "One who is endowed with the eight enclosures and devoted to the five modes of conduct..."
One should perform Vedic ritual action, which is the means for accomplishing the single fruit that is knowledge.
He who, having placed his desired own *liṅga* upon the palm of his hand, has the movement of his mind absorbed therein;
O dear one, he whose soul is free from desire for the multitude of external activities—he indeed is a Vīraśaiva. || 10 ||
Animals are superior in intelligence to worms, insects, and moths.
Men are superior even to animals; among them, the twice-born are the most excellent.
Among the twice-born, the Brahmins are superior; among the Brahmins, those whose intellects are fixed on sacrifice are superior.
Among those whose intellects are fixed on ritual acts, the renunciants are superior. || 12 ||
Among them, the wise are superior; among the wise, those who worship Śaṅkara are the best.
Among them, O fortunate one, the most excellent are those who are united with my own body as their liṅga.
One who possesses knowledge of the six stages (ṣaṭsthalajñāna) becomes superior even among those whose limbs are in contact with the Liṅga.
Therefore, there is no one superior to him at any time throughout the three worlds. || 14 ||
He is always to be saluted and worshipped by those who desire to conquer the cycle of worldly existence.
What is the use of saying much more, my child? I am that very person; of this there is no doubt.
In the Pārameśvara-āgama.
He who has sacred ash upon his forehead and a linga made of my own substance around his neck.
O Goddess, he who wears Rudrākṣa ornaments on his body is none other than I; of this there is no doubt.
Thus, by the force of such authoritative means of knowledge, the supreme excellence of the Vīraśaivas is established. || 17 ||
Is it not so?
One who has fallen away from the Vedas becomes filled with fear regarding the expiatory rites prescribed by the Vedas.
In due order, for the sake of attaining the Śruti, a human being should take recourse to the Manuṣya-tantra.
Thus, that tantra should never be practiced by those men who have strayed from the path of the Vedas, nor indeed by those who are devoted to the path of the Vedas. 19.
For those men who have utterly strayed from the path of the Vedas, indeed.
The paths such as Pāñcarātra and others are beneficial only for a limited time.
The Kāpāla, the Pāñcarātra, the Yāmala, the Vāma, and the Ārhata.
And there are other such things as these, intended for the purpose of delusion.
And those who eat excrement, whoever they may be, adorned with ornaments made of human skulls.
The Śaivas, the Pāśupatas, others, as well as the Pāñcarātras.
Likewise, all other evil-minded ones, including both asuras and deities, [were likewise struck]. || 22 ||
The word *pāśa* is traditionally understood as the Dharma of the three Vedas, because it protects the world.
Because those heretics (pāṣaṇḍas) break that [tradition], for that reason...
Since the adoption of the path of the *kevala-tantra* alone is censured by such statements from the *Kūrma*, *Brahmavaivarta*, *Sūta-saṃhitā*, *Vāsiṣṭha*, *Laiṅga*, and *Parāśara Upapurāṇas*,
and since the duties to be performed by Vīraśaivas are prescribed only in such *tantras* and not among the Vedic [texts],...

If it is argued, "How can the superiority of the Vīraśaivas—who are solely intent on the performance of such duties—be established, given that they are not seen even in the Śruti, Smṛti, and Itihāsas?", do not say so. || 24 ||
Sāṃkhya, Yoga, Pāñcarātra, Veda, and likewise Pāśupata.
These are equal in measure to the Self; they must not be destroyed by means of arguments.

Thus, from this statement in the *Anuśāsana-parvan* of the *Mahābhārata*, since the Pāñcarātra and other Āgamas— which have been censured by other Purāṇas— attain the status of being authoritative, it is established that the duties proclaimed therein must necessarily be performed. || 26 ||

And even if, by virtue of the statement in the *Bhārata*, the conclusion is reached that only the *Pāñcarātra* and *Pāśupata* dharmas are to be practiced, how [is this so] given that the *Vīraśaiva* dharmas are not included within the *Pāśupatas*?
It should be stated that there is excellence for those who are intent upon the practice of those dharmas. || 27 ||

Appayya Dīkṣita established that the Pāśupata system is twofold, divided into Vedic and non-Vedic; that the prohibitive statements refer specifically to the non-Vedic Pāśupatas, while the prescriptive statements refer to the Vedic Pāśupatas and Vīraśaivas.

In the *Parimala* commentary on the *Kalpataru*, within the section titled "The Lord’s lack of propriety" (*patyurasāmañjasyāt*), after discussing the various Pāśupata sects, the author declared that the *Laguḍīśa-Pāśupata* is to be accepted.

Therefore, the tantric nature of the Vīraśaiva doctrines does not constitute the delimiting factor for their rejection. Now, even though Appayya Dīkṣita, in his *Parimala*, established that the Lakuṭīśa-Pāśupata system is to be accepted as Vedic, [the same applies to] the Āgamas that propound the Vīraśaiva doctrines.
If it is argued that because they are distinct from the inclusion within the Laguḍīśa-Pāśupata [tradition], they must ultimately be rejected as non-Vedic, we say no. || 28 ||
In the Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi: "Because they establish the same meaning, there is unity between the Veda and the Siddhānta;
the wise should always recognize that the authority of these two is equal. (29)
In the Kriyāsāra:
Alternatively, those Śiva-āgamas are superior to the Vedas because they issued directly from the mouth of Śiva himself. (30)
The Nigamas and Āgamas spoken by Śiva have mutually non-contradictory meanings;
yet those of small intellect imagine mutual contradictions between them. (31)
The authority of both the Nigamas and the Āgamas must be understood without distinction by those who perceive the truth, on the basis of the instruction of the supreme authoritative teacher. 32.

Thus, because the authority [of the Purāṇas] must be accepted by the learned— given that they establish the duties of the castes and stages of life not contrary to the Vedas and possess a single authorship by the Supreme Lord, who is the most trustworthy of all—
it is established that all practices prescribed in those scriptures are to be performed by the followers of the Veda. || 33 ||
Otherwise,

[there would be failure] regarding the construction of temples for deities such as Śiva, the consecration of Śivaliṅgas and other icons, the rituals for chariot festivals and the like, the extraction of mantras, the defects of mantras, the purification of mantras, the ritual placement of mantras (nyāsa), and the application of mudrās.
The engagement of those who follow the Veda would not occur if it were based solely on the Śiva-āgamas. || 34 ||

Furthermore, in the *Sūta-saṃhitā*, within the *Śivamāhātmya-khaṇḍa*, during the section concerning the reliability of Vyāsa’s words, it is stated: "The son of Satyavatī is the author of the eighteen Purāṇas."
Just as the Lord Maheśvara is [the source] of the various divisions beginning with the Kāmika; || 35 ||
Thus [it is said]. In the commentary on that, the venerable Vidyāraṇya,

in order to engender confidence in the words of Vyāsa, begins with the number eighteen and establishes the authority of the Śaiva Āgamas, such as the Kāmika and others, precisely because they were spoken by Śiva.

Thus, it has been established that the eighteen Purāṇas composed by Vyāsa—an incarnation of Nārāyaṇa—are authoritative; therefore, the necessity of practicing the Vīraśaiva duties taught in those Āgamas is proven. || 36 ||

And thus, among the seven types of Śaivas distinguished in their respective scriptures as *anādiśaiva*, *ādiśaiva*, *mahāśaiva*, *anuśaiva*, *avāntaraśaiva*, *pravaraśaiva*, and *antyasaiva*—who are differentiated by variations in their conduct (*ācāra*)— [The text continues: ...among these... [the specific point or subject follows].
Among the fourfold types— namely Sāmānyaśaiva, Miśraśaiva, Śuddhaśaiva, and Vīraśaiva—
the Vīraśaiva is further divided into three categories according to differences in practice: Sāmānyavīraśaiva, Viśeṣavīraśaiva, and Nirābhāravīraśaiva.

Furthermore, the uncommon Vīraśaiva duties— consisting of the application of sacred ash (*bhasma*), the wearing of *rudrākṣa* beads, the recitation of the five-syllabled mantra (*pañcākṣarī*), the wearing of the *liṅga*, the worship of the Guru as the *liṅga* and as the *aṅga*, and the acceptance of the water from his feet (*pādodaka*) and his grace—
are established in such Upaniṣads as the *Kālāgnirudra*, *Bhasmajābāla*, *Cidambaravedāntasāra*, and others.
In the Bṛhat-taittirīya and other mantras that establish the wearing of the *liṅga*,
in the Śaṅkarasaṃhitā, Sūtasaṃhitā, Śivarahaśya, Liṅgapurāṇa, and others,
and in the twenty-eight Śaiva Āgamas beginning with the Kāmika and ending with the Vātula;
And because they exist among those Vīraśaivas who are called Ārādhya and have been described [above], their status as followers of the Vedas (Vaidika) is established. || 37 ||

Otherwise, those Brāhmaṇas who are considered Vaidikas, yet perform Tantric rites such as chariot festivals and consecrations, would not possess the status of being Vaidikas; and thus, by the same logic, the aforementioned Vaidika status remains secure. || 38 ||

Now, [one might ask]: regarding the Śrutis and Āgamas that propound the Vīraśaiva dharma—which, according to differences in practice, are designated as *sāmānya*, *viśeṣa*, and *nirābhāsa*; which consist of the stages of *bhakta*, *māheśvara*, *prasādin*, *prāṇaliṅgin*, and *śaraṇaikya*; and which concern the *ācāraliṅga* and *guruliṅga*—[how can there be a single doctrine?]

Because the practice of successive dharmas at the Liṅga-sthalas— namely those designated as Aśiva-liṅga, Jaṅgama-liṅga, Prasāda-liṅga, and Mahā-liṅga— as well as at the previously mentioned Aṅga-sthalas, occurs in a sequential manner following the practice of each preceding dharma, such is the nature of the practice of those dharmas.

If it is argued that [the text] cannot have as its subject matter only those other than the Ārādhya [class of Vīraśaivas], because it can be interpreted as referring to the supreme object of worship who is devoted to the performance of a synthesis of Vedic and Āgamic duties—such as wearing the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) and bearing the *liṅga*—while residing in regions like Kālahasti and Śrīśaila, we say: no. (39)
He fully proclaimed this supreme purifier, which is cherished by the assembly of sages, to those who have transcended the stages of life (atyāśramins).
In the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad, verse 40.
And in the Kaivalya Upaniṣad it is said: "One who has transcended the stages of life (atyāśramī) should recite [the mantra] either constantly or once. (41)
Regarding the term *atyāśramin* as it is heard [in scripture]: "The student, the householder, the forest-dweller, and the mendicant."
And the one who transcends the castes and stages of life (ativarṇāśramī); these are the wise ones, superior in their respective order. || 42 ||
O Lotus-eyed One, even a householder is superior to one who dwells in the forest and to an ascetic.
One becomes a guru solely by the power of the excellence of one's knowledge, and not otherwise. || 43 ||
O Hari, even one established in the stage of the forest-dweller (vānaprastha) as well as a renunciant (saṃnyāsī) [is likewise].
One becomes a guru only through the power of the excellence of knowledge, and not otherwise.
The Guru who transcends all castes and stages of life is declared to be the authority for all qualified seekers.
Even he would not be superior to me, O Supreme Person, as I have said.
One who transcends the castes and stages of life is said to be the manifest teacher of even teachers.
He for whom the conduct of the castes and stages of life has dissolved through the vision of his own Self.
Having transcended all the stages of life (āśramas) appropriate to his own caste, he abides in his own self.
That man who, having transcended his own stages of life and social classes, abides in the Self alone.
Thus he is declared by those who expound the meaning of all the Vedas to be one who has transcended the [ordinary] castes and stages of life (ativarṇāśramī). || 47 ||
The five-syllabled supreme knowledge leads to the attainment of the light of Śiva.
The syllable *oṃ* is the *praṇava*, the manifest and supreme seed of all vidyās.
Therefore, one should purify all principles without exception by means of the Praṇava. || 49 ||
One should smear the body with ashes using the seven mantras beginning with "agniriti."
One should apply the triple mark (tripuṇḍraka) with the mantra: "The triple life-span of Jamadagni."
One should contemplate within oneself Śambhu, the Lord, the supreme Śiva, the peaceful one, accompanied by Umā.
They call this one whose limbs are covered in ashes and whose radiant body is revealed the "Atyāśrama" (Beyond-Asceticism) practice.
This is the supreme stage of life among all four stages of life.
That which is an animal, and its state of being an animal—one should abandon both through this vow. || 52 ||
Or again, having purified all the principles (tattvas) with the syllable Om (praṇava).
And having established my own self within me, the stainless Supreme Lord.
One should bathe one's own body with that very water of knowledge.
This is the Pāśupata yoga for the sake of liberation from the bonds of the individual soul (paśu).
"This is the essence of all Vedānta, known as Atyāśrama," so says the Śruti.
By whom the Pāśupata vow was correctly observed with joy.
His knowledge shall arise, and by that there is liberation from the bonds.

Thus, by such statements from the Kāmika, Skānda, Liṅga, and Śiva Āgamas, it is established that those who have transcended the stages of life (ati-varṇāśramin) are superior to those whose nature is to practice the duties of their respective castes and stages of life (varṇāśrama-dharma).

Since the status of being "beyond the stages of life" (atyāśramatva) culminates in the Vīraśaiva Brāhmaṇas who possess the fifth stage of life arising from the Five-Faced One (Pañcamukha), there is no room for the suspicion that it refers to the previously mentioned object of worship. || 56 ||

For this very reason, the statement from the Śāṅkarasaṃhitā beginning with "from the aforementioned worms, insects, and birds," which establishes the superiority of Vīraśaiva, results in being unerring. || 57 ||
But is it not the case that the scriptural, traditional, and puranic statements establishing the "beyond-the-ashram" (atyāśrama) do not terminate in those [very states]?
However, they culminate in those Brahmins who observe the conduct of their caste and stage of life (varṇāśrama), as well as in those beyond them who are worthy of worship. 58.
For instance, regarding the phrase "transcending the conduct of the castes and stages of life" (*ativarṇāśramācāra*), there are four castes: Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, and Śūdra.
For those who are not Śūdras and whose actions are not corrupt, the initiation ceremony, Vedic study, the establishment of the sacred fires, and the fruit-bearing rituals are appropriate.
There are four stages of life (āśrama), distinguished as studenthood (brahmacarya), householdership (gārhasthya), forest-dwelling (vānaprastha), and renunciation (saṃnyāsitva).

Among these, the duties of the first stage consist of residing in the teacher’s house, wandering for alms, studying the Vedas, and so forth; [the duties of the second stage consist of] the domestic rites beginning with the impregnation ceremony (garbhādhāna), the seven pākayajñas, the seven haviryajñas, and the seven saṃsthā-yajñas.
The forty-eight sacraments (saṃskāras) consist of the five great sacrifices (pañcamahāyajña).

Furthermore, the six duties consisting of sacrificing for oneself, officiating at sacrifices for others, studying, teaching, giving gifts, and receiving gifts are the dharmas of the second stage of life (āśrama). || 60 ||

The duty of the third stage of life (the forest-dweller) consists of subsisting on a diet of wild rice, roots, and fruits, as well as the observance of ascetic practices such as wearing matted hair and deerskins, and performing the kṛcchra and cāndrāyaṇa penances.

The dharma of the fourth stage of life (turīyāśrama) consists of abandoning the duties of the three previously mentioned stages, followed by the investigation of Brahman, the practice of begging for alms, the avoidance of passion, hatred, and the like, the restraint of speech, dwelling in solitude, and the practice of yoga. || 62 ||

Regarding the expression *ativarṇāśramācāra*, the meaning of the word should be construed according to the rules of grammar (*vyākaraṇānuśāsana*) which state that "prefixes such as *ati* [govern] the accusative case when they have the sense of 'transcending' (*krānta*) and so forth"— namely, *atikrānto varṇāśramācārān*. Furthermore, this refers to those who possess the practice of the aforementioned dharmas.
How can the application of words such as "excessive" (*ati*), which depend on the presence of a counter-correlative (*pratiyogi*),
be justified when used— without reference to that counter-correlative— in relation to Vīraśaivas who are distinct from those to be worshipped? This applies equally to words expressive of prohibition.
If it is argued that [the word] ought to apply only to those things characterized by the possibility of a relation with a counter-correlative, we say no. || 63 ||
Those who transcend the conduct of the castes and stages of life arise from the upward-facing mouth.
They indeed rejoice directly in Mahādeva and in the Āgamas.
Just as those with five faces, such as Pañcāsya, were born, so too were others superior to them.
"Those who are my devotees are always dear to me, even more so than those of all other castes. (65)
The Liṅga is Śiva, the body is the field (kṣetra), and their union is the substratum (āśraya).
Therefore, even one who is joined with the limbs of the *liṅga* shall become a person of supreme austerity (*atyāmaśramī*). || 66 ||
Born from the lineage of the Gaṇas from the mouth of Īśāna, they possess the splendor of the Liṅga and the body, being solely devoted to the path of liberation.
The state of identity between the *liṅga* and the body, and the wearing of the *liṅga* upon the body.
By performing this very rite, they were indeed liberated from the bonds of saṃsāra.
Thus,

by means of such statements from the *Kāmika* and other Āgamas, as well as the *Kriyāsāra*, the *Udāhṛta-vedāntasāra-upaniṣad*, and others, it is properly established that the term "Vīraśaiva" is conventionally denotative of those who follow the conduct of being beyond the [standard] castes and stages of life (*ativarṇāśrama*).

Because it is possible [to understand it otherwise]. Furthermore, the statement that the word *atyāśramin* does not apply to those who have performed the duties of their stage of life (*āśrama*) because it is a relative term (*pratiyogika-śabda*) is untenable. For Vedic words such as *apahatapāpmā* ("one whose evil has been struck away") would have no application with respect to Brahman, since the "evils" (*pāpman*) that serve as their correlates are impossible in Brahman's case.
Likewise,

because there is an absence of anyone capable of performing the duties of the four castes and stages of life (*caturvarṇāśrama-dharma*), it is consistent that they are designated by such terms as *atyāśrama* (beyond the stages of life) and so forth. Nor does this contradict the grammatical rule regarding words beginning with *ati*.
It should be stated.

Just as in the cases of Śuka, Vāmadeva, and others, there is no contradiction with the grammarians' instruction because one can postulate the performance of the duties of caste and stage of life belonging to previous births. || 68 ||

Nor should it be argued that, if the etymological consistency of the term *atyāśramin* were established in this manner, it would follow that others besides Vīraśaivas— namely, other renunciants, men of knowledge, and even Śūdras— would also possess the status of *atyāśramins*. (69)

Regarding the term *atyāśramin*, which possesses a conventional meaning as understood from the three scriptural statements beginning with "one who transcends the conduct of caste and stage of life" (*ativarṇāśramācāra*),

it is improper for it to function through mere etymology (*yoga*)— as in the case of the word *paṅkaja* [meaning "born in mud"] referring to grass or a blue lotus— according to the maxim that "conventionality sets aside etymological derivation. (70)

For this very reason, according to the rule of the sūtra *anahaḥ khakratau*, the word *ahīna*—which denotes a series of sacrificial days (*ahargaṇa*) and refers specifically to sacrifices accomplished over two or three nights and so forth—is not "deficient" (*hīna*). Thus, by the etymological derivation (*yoga*) that it is "not deficient" (*ahīna*), and by Vedic scriptural authority (*śruti*), it does not refer to another type of sacrifice; therefore, it is indeed the *ahīna*.
In the section concerning "at the beginning of the treatise" (*prakaraṇādau*), this very principle has been established in the third chapter of the *Pūrvatantra*.
Therefore, the term *atyāśramin* (one who has transcended the stages of life) is applicable to the Vīraśaivas. || 71 ||
Alternatively, even by means of the power of yogic interpretation, it is possible to conceive of this as being directed toward Vīraśaivism.
For instance, according to the *Amarakośa*, which states that "tu, hi, ca, sma, ha, and vai" are used for filling a verse (*pādapūraṇa*) or for honor (*pūjana*),

and by the rule "śva-ti" [is used] in the sense of honor (*pūjā*), the etymological derivation is: those whose conduct (*ācāra*) according to their caste and stage of life (*varṇāśrama*) is exceedingly honored (*atiśayita-pūjita*).

Nor do these statements refer to the status of being a "transcendent ascetic" (atyāśramin), which consists of the wearing of ashes and rudrākṣa beads— a practice synonymous with the Pāśupata system— preceded by the ritual procedure prescribed in the *Atharvaṇa-śiras* and the *Jābāla*.
Whether it be one who has abandoned all latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) preceded by the knowledge of his own Self;
whether he is devoid of or possessed of the wearing of sectarian marks (*liṅga*) and so forth;
whether he is a Brahmin worthy of worship or merely an ordinary person.
It should not be said that these [terms] express a connection with the state of being beyond the stages of life (atyāśramitva), rather than merely denoting Vīraśaiva. || 72 ||

Because those who observe the duties of the castes and stages of life (*varṇāśrama-dharma*) and have propitiated Brahmins are worthy of being designated by the term "one who has transcended the stages of life" (*atyāśramin*),
[he is] the leader of the host of attendants (*pramatha-gaṇa-nāyaka*) born from the five faces of the Supreme Lord, namely Ghaṇṭākarṇa, Gajakarṇa, and Reṇu.

For it is appropriate that the term "atyāśramin" (one who has transcended the stages of life) be applied only to the exclusive Vīraśaivas— who are born from the lineages of Kadāruka and Viśvakarṇa and who practice solely the duties of the super-classes and super-stages— as established by the aforementioned Śrutis, Āgamas, and Purāṇas. || 73 ||
Furthermore, since the Pramathas—
who have emerged from the five faces of the Supreme Lord (Parameśvara) and are His most intimate attendants—
do not take wives of ordinary human nature as do common men, how could they possibly be born of such a lineage?
Nevertheless, if it does exist, then it must be stated that even the Brahmins who are to be propitiated are born of that same lineage.
To Dvārāpā, who touches [the water], Svāhā! To Dvārāpī, who touches [the water], Svāhā!
To Dvārāpī, Svāhā!

Thus, since Nandikeśvara— who is designated by the term *dvārāpaśabda*— and his wife Suyaśādevī are well-known and established in the Purāṇas and other texts as being present for the sake of bestowing grace upon the world during the ritual known as the Īśānabalī, [this is performed] for the Supreme Lord...

Just as there is the assumption of forms such as that of a Kirāta, the possibility of taking a wife from the common folk (prākṛta) implies that even for those who are purely Vīraśaivas, birth in such a lineage is possible; however, for those Brahmins who are to be worshipped, birth in such a lineage is in every way improper. || 75 ||
If it is argued that those who take pride in following the Vīraśaiva dharma possess descent from those [sages],
